voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
He was a real man, not an idea. One of us, Ignatius, wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup, we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

One of us, Ignatius, calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

results.message: were there other voices from your world that spoke about Jesus?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
Yes. We need to tell you plainly that there were. 

One teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of the older scriptures harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

There was also a movement some called the New Prophecy, spreading among churches in Asia near the very end of our own time. Churches there met - often, and in many places - over whether to receive it. And there were teachers like Valentinus, whose own followers were our neighbors, not people far away.

We have to be honest about what this means: Marcion, Valentinian teaching, and the New Prophecy were live, contemporary, geographically overlapping neighbors. The boundary against them was being drawn in real time. The settled lines that came later must never be read back into our own world.

sources.work: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles); final form c. 80-120 CE per Niederwimmer (outer range to 150 CE; Milavec's minority view argues unified composition 50-70 CE)
sources.locus: 1-6 (the Two Ways as one community's own primary catechetical mode: concrete, direct instruction rather than difficult narrative - representativeness limit applies, see body)

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130-c. 202 CE; formed in Smyrna under Polycarp, writing from Gaul c. 180)
sources.work: Adversus Haereses (Against Heresies); a BOUNDARY WITNESS in two senses: its Book I is the fullest contemporary description of Valentinian teaching (hostile, but the principal source), and its four-Gospel, apostolic-succession argument is itself one of the three markers of this world's own closing (Doc_01 SS2.2) - a new systematic mode this world's voices do not yet speak
sources.locus: Book I, ch. 27 (Marcion's rejection of the Jewish scriptures' God as harsh and self-contradictory, and his own mutilation of Luke's Gospel and Paul's letters, per this hostile witness)

sources.work: First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Clement); traditionally c. 96 CE - the date is actively contested (Welborn broadens the plausible range to 80-140 CE; Herron's minority position argues pre-70)
sources.locus: 42, 44 (the authority dispute at Corinth)

sources.author: Ignatius of Antioch (if the traditional attribution holds - see the three-way dispute below)
sources.work: The seven letters, middle recension (Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, To Polycarp); traditional dating c. 107-117 CE, redated 130s-140s by Barnes and Foster, held pseudepigraphic c. 160-180 by Huebner and Lechner - a genuine three-way scholarly split
sources.locus: passim (the monarchical-bishop program)

sources.author: The 'Anonymous' anti-Montanist (writing c. 192-193 CE to Avircius Marcellus), preserved only in Eusebius's quotations; ANF prints the fragments under the conjectural name 'Asterius Urbanus'
sources.work: Fragments against the Montanists (the New Prophecy) - the earliest sustained inside-the-window testimony to Montanism's Phrygian origin, its spread, and the synodical opposition of Asia Minor's churches; the movement's start date is disputed between c. 157 (Epiphanius) and c. 172 (Eusebius's implied chronology), with current scholarship favoring the later end
sources.locus: the synodical opposition of Asia Minor's churches, near this world's own closing edge

sentences.sentence: One teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of the older scriptures harsh and self-contradictory.
He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it.
We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: We did not follow him there.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: There was also a movement some called the New Prophecy, spreading among churches in Asia near the very end of our own time.
Churches there met - often, and in many places - over whether to receive it.
And there were teachers like Valentinus, whose own followers were our neighbors, not people far away.
We have to be honest about what this means: Marcion, Valentinian teaching, and the New Prophecy were live, contemporary, geographically overlapping neighbors.
The boundary against them was being drawn in real time.
The settled lines that came later must never be read back into our own world.
